source_text: Οὔπω γὰρ ταῦτα ἐγεγόνει. Ὥστε οὐχ ἁμαρτήσεις τῆς ἀληθείας, κἂν τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀκατάσκευον εἴπῃς. Ἀόρατον δὲ τὴν γῆν προσεῖπε διὰ δύο αἰτίας· ἢ ὅτι οὔπω ἦν αὐτῆς ὁ θεατὴς ἄνθρωπος, ἢ ὅτι ὑποβρύχιος οὖσα ἐκ τοῦ ἐπιπολάζοντος τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ ὕδατος οὐκ ἠδύνατο καθορᾶσθαι. Οὔπω γὰρ ἦν συναχθέντα τὰ ὕδατα εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα συστήματα, ἅπερ ὕστερον ὁ Θεὸς συναγαγὼν προσηγόρευσε θαλάσσας. Ἀόρατον οὖν τί ἐστι; Τὸ μὲν, ὃ μὴ πέφυκεν ὀφθαλμοῖς σαρκὸς καθορᾶσθαι, ὡς ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἡμέτερος· τὸ δὲ, ὃ τῇ φύσει ὁρατὸν ὑπάρχον, διὰ τὴν ἐπιπρόσθεσιν τοῦ ἐπικειμένου αὐτῷ σώματος ἀποκρύπτεται, ὡς ὁ ἐν τῷ βυθῷ σίδηρος. Καθ' ὃ σημαινόμενον νῦν ἀόρατον ἡγούμεθα προσειρῆσθαι τὴν γῆν καλυπτομένην ὑπὸ τοῦ ὕδατος. Ἔπειτα μέντοι, καὶ μήπω τοῦ φωτὸς γενηθέντος, οὐδὲν ἦν θαυμαστὸν τὴν ἐν σκότῳ κειμένην, διὰ τὸ ἀφώτιστον εἶναι τὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς ἀέρα, ἀόρατον καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο παρὰ τῆς Γραφῆς προσειρῆσθαι. 2.2 Ἀλλ' οἱ παραχαράκται τῆς ἀληθείας, οἱ οὐχὶ τῇ Γραφῇ τὸν ἑαυτῶν νοῦν ἀκολουθεῖν ἐκδιδάσκοντες, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον βούλημα τὴν διάνοιαν τῶν Γραφῶν διαστρέφοντες, τὴν ὕλην φασὶ διὰ τῶν λέξεων τούτων παραδηλοῦσθαι. Αὕτη γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ ἀόρατος τῇ φύσει καὶ ἀκατα σκεύαστος, ἄποιος οὖσα τῷ ἑαυτῆς λόγῳ, καὶ παντὸς εἴδους καὶ σχήματος κεχωρισμένη, ἣν παραλαβὼν ὁ τεχνίτης τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σοφίᾳ ἐμόρφωσε, καὶ εἰς τάξιν ἤγαγε, καὶ οὕτω δι' αὐτῆς οὐσίωσε τὰ ὁρώμενα. Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀγέννητος αὕτη, πρῶτον μὲν ὁμότιμος τῷ Θεῷ, τῶν αὐτῶν πρεσβείων ἀξιουμένη. Οὗ τί ἂν γένοιτο ἀσεβέστερον, τὴν ἄποιον, τὴν ἀνείδεον, τὴν ἐσχάτην ἀμορφίαν, τὸ ἀδιατύπωτον αἶσχος (τοῖς γὰρ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων προσρήμασι κέχρημαι) τῆς αὐτῆς προεδρίας ἀξιοῦσθαι τῷ σοφῷ καὶ δυνατῷ καὶ παγκάλῳ δημιουργῷ καὶ κτίστῃ τῶν ὅλων; Ἔπειτα εἰ μὲν τοσαύτη ἐστὶν, ὥστε ὅλην ὑποδέχεσθαι τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν ἐπιστήμην· καὶ οὕτω, τρόπον τινὰ, τῇ ἀνεξιχνιάστῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμει ἀντιπαρεξάγουσιν αὐτῆς τὴν ὑπόστασιν, εἴπερ ἐξαρκεῖ ὅλην τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν σύνεσιν δι' ἑαυτῆς ἐκμετρεῖν· εἰ δὲ ἐλάττων ἡ ὕλη τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐνεργείας, καὶ οὕτως εἰς ἀτοπωτέραν βλασφημίαν αὐτοῖς ὁ λόγος περιτραπήσεται, δι' ἔνδειαν ὕλης ἄπρακτον καὶ ἀνενέργητον τῶν οἰκείων ἔργων τὸν Θεὸν κατεχόντων. Ἀλλ' ἐξηπάτησε γὰρ αὐτοὺς τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως ἡ πενία. Καὶ ἐπειδὴ παρ' ἡμῖν ἑκάστη τέχνη περί τινα ὕλην ἀφωρισμένως ἠσχόληται, οἷον χαλευτικὴ μὲν περὶ τὸν σίδηρον, τεκτονικὴ δὲ περὶ τὰ ξύλα· καὶ ἐν τούτοις ἄλλο μέν τί ἐστι τὸ ὑποκείμενον, ἄλλο δὲ τὸ εἶδος, ἄλλο δὲ τὸ ἐκ τοῦ εἴδους ἀποτελούμενον· καὶ ἔστιν ἡ μὲν ὕλη ἔξωθεν παραλαμβανομένη, τὸ δὲ εἶδος παρὰ τῆς τέχνης ἐφαρμοζόμενον, ἀποτέλεσμα δὲ τὸ ἐξ ἀμφοῖν συντιθέμενον ἔκ τε τοῦ εἴδους καὶ τῆς ὕλης· οὕτως οἴονται καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς θείας δημιουργίας, τὸ μὲν σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου παρὰ τῆς σοφίας ἐπῆχθαι τοῦ ποιητοῦ τῶν ὅλων, τὴν δὲ ὕλην ἔξωθεν ὑποβεβλῆσθαι τῷ κτίσαντι, καὶ γεγε νῆσθαι τὸν κόσμον σύνθετον, τὸ μὲν ὑποκείμενον καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἑτέρωθεν ἔχοντα, τὸ δὲ σχῆμα καὶ τὴν μορφὴν παρὰ Θεοῦ προσλαβόντα.
thought_title: Why the earth is called invisible; against those who posit uncreated matter
orientation: Basil is explaining the phrase 'invisible and unformed' from Genesis 1:2, and now turns to refute interpreters who claim it refers to eternal, uncreated matter.
pass_a_gloss: For these things had not yet come to be. So you will not miss the truth, even if you call the heaven unformed. And he called the earth invisible for two reasons: either because man, its beholder, did not yet exist, or because, being under water, from the water spreading over its surface it could not be seen. For the waters had not yet been gathered into their own gatherings, which later God, having gathered them, named seas. What then is invisible? One thing is what is not by nature able to be seen by eyes of flesh, such as our mind; another thing is what, being by nature visible, is hidden because of the covering of the body lying upon it, such as iron in the deep. According to which meaning we now consider the earth to have been called invisible, being covered by the water. Then indeed, also, since light had not yet come to be, it was no wonder that the earth lying in darkness, because the air above it was unlit, was called invisible also for this reason by the Scripture. But the counterfeiters of the truth, those who do not teach their own mind to follow the Scripture, but twist the meaning of the Scriptures toward their own wish, say that matter is indicated through these words. For this, they say, is both invisible by nature and unformed, being without quality by its own account, and separated from every form and shape, which the craftsman, taking it over, formed by his own wisdom, and brought into order, and thus through it gave substance to the visible things. If then this matter is unbegotten, first it is equal in honor to God, being deemed worthy of the same privileges. Than which what could be more impious, that the qualityless, the formless, the utter shapelessness, the unformed ugliness (for I use their own terms) be deemed worthy of the same preeminence as the wise and powerful and all-beautiful craftsman and creator of all things? Then if it is so great as to receive the whole knowledge of God, then in this way, in a certain manner, they set its substance alongside the unsearchable power of God, if indeed it suffices to measure out through itself the whole understanding of God; but if matter is less than the energy of God, then in this way their argument will turn into a more absurd blasphemy, since they hold God back from his own works as inactive and ineffective through lack of matter. But the poverty of human nature deceived them. And since among us each art is occupied with some matter in a defined way, such as metalworking with iron, and carpentry with wood; and in these one thing is the underlying thing, another is the form, another is what is completed from the form; and the matter is taken from outside, and the form is fitted on by the art, and the result is what is composed from both, from the form and the matter; so they think also in the case of the divine creation, that the shape of the world was brought on by the wisdom of the maker of all things, but the matter was supplied from outside to the creator, and that the world came to be composite, having the underlying thing and the substance from elsewhere, but receiving the shape and the form from God.

choices.why: The term means those who falsify or debase, like counterfeiters of coin; it captures Basil's charge that they corrupt the genuine meaning of Scripture.
Basil is attacking the philosophical concept of pre-existent, uncreated matter; 'matter' is the standard English term for this technical concept.
The term means ungenerated or uncreated; 'unbegotten' preserves the theological force of the Greek, distinguishing it from created things.
The verb means to bring in alongside for comparison; it conveys the heretics' move of placing matter's substance on a par with God's power.
Basil is using his opponents' own derogatory terms ironically; 'unformed ugliness' preserves the rhetorical force of the phrase.

bible_refs.note: Basil is expounding the words 'invisible and unformed' (ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος) from Genesis 1:2, and the gathering of waters named seas from Genesis 1:9-10.

pass_b_english: For none of these things had yet come to be. So you will not stray from the truth if you say that the heaven too was unformed. Scripture calls the earth invisible for two reasons: either because there was not yet a human being to see it, or because it lay submerged beneath the water spreading over its surface and could not be seen. The waters had not yet been gathered into their own gatherings, which God later gathered together and named seas. What then is invisible? One kind is what is not by nature able to be seen by the eyes of flesh, like our mind. Another kind is what is visible by nature but is hidden because a body covering it stands in the way, like iron in the deep. In this latter sense we understand the earth to be called invisible now, since it was covered by the water. And further, since light had not yet come to be, it was no wonder that Scripture also called the earth invisible for this reason: it lay in darkness, because the air above it was unlit.

But the counterfeiters of the truth—those who do not train their own minds to follow Scripture, but twist the meaning of the Scriptures toward their own wish—say that matter is indicated by these words. For this, they say, is by nature both invisible and unformed: without quality in its own right, separated from every form and shape. The craftsman, they say, took it in hand, shaped it by his own wisdom, brought it into order, and so through it gave being to the visible world. Now if this matter is unbegotten, then first of all it is equal in honor to God, deemed worthy of the same privileges. What could be more impious than this—that the qualityless, the formless, the uttermost formlessness, the unformed ugliness (I am using their own terms) should be deemed worthy of the same preeminence as the wise and powerful and all-beautiful craftsman and creator of all things? And further, if matter is so great as to receive the whole knowledge of God, then in some way they set its substance alongside the unsearchable power of God—if indeed it is sufficient to measure out through itself the whole understanding of God. But if matter is less than God's activity, then their argument turns into an even more absurd blasphemy: they would have God held back from his own works, ineffective and inactive, for lack of matter.

But the poverty of human nature has deceived them. Among us, every craft is occupied with some particular matter—metalworking with iron, carpentry with wood—and in these things one thing is the underlying material, another the form, and another the finished product that results from the form. The matter is taken from outside, the form is applied by the craft, and the finished product is what is composed from both, from the form and the matter. So they suppose it is also with the divine creation: the shape of the world was brought in by the wisdom of the maker of all things, but the matter was supplied from outside to the creator, and the world came to be composite—having its underlying substance and being from elsewhere, but receiving its shape and form from God.

problems.quote: having its underlying substance and being from one source
problems.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὑποκείμενον καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἑτέρωθεν ἔχοντα
problems.why: ἑτέρωθεν means 'from another/source elsewhere'—'from one source' is wrong; it means from a different/source other than God, i.e., matter has its substance from elsewhere, not from God.
problems.fix: having its underlying substance and essence from elsewhere
problems.ruling: ἑτέρωθεν means 'from another/elsewhere,' not 'from one source.' Contrasts with παρὰ Θεοῦ; loses the anti-cosmological argument.

edits.old: having its underlying substance and being from one source
edits.new: having its underlying substance and being from elsewhere

fixed: Corrected 'from one source' to 'from elsewhere' to match ἑτέρωθεν, which means 'from another place/source,' not 'from one source.'

last_rejected.why: Source says heaven was 'unformed/unfurnished' (ἀκατάσκευον), not 'too'—no comparison to earth's state is made here.
last_rejected.fix: So you will not stray from the truth if you say that heaven was unformed.
last_rejected.ruling: 'too' reflects καὶ before τὸν οὐρανὸν; ἀκατάσκευον = unformed/unfurnished, correctly rendered.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'he called the earth invisible' (Moses/God as speaker), not 'Scripture calls'—agency shifted to text.
last_rejected.fix: He called the earth invisible for two reasons
last_rejected.ruling: προσεῖπε lacks explicit subject; 'Scripture calls' is standard paraphrase for biblical reference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: The waters had not yet been gathered into their own gatherings
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὔπω γὰρ ἦν συναχθέντα τὰ ὕδατα εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα συστήματα
last_rejected.why: Missing 'for' (γὰρ) causal link explaining why earth was invisible—waters not yet gathered because not yet gathered into own systems.
last_rejected.fix: For the waters had not yet been gathered into their own gatherings
last_rejected.ruling: γὰρ is a minor discourse particle; its causal force is implicit in context, not a meaning-changing omission.

last_rejected.quote: the finished product that results from the form
last_rejected.why: Source says 'what is completed from/out of the form'—not 'results from the form' but the product that comes from (both, implied) the form (and matter).
last_rejected.fix: another the finished product completed from the form
last_rejected.ruling: 'results from the form' is within normal range for ἀποτελούμενον; next clause specifies 'from both,' so no misleading.

last_rejected.quote: having its underlying substance and being from elsewhere
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὑποκείμενον καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἑτέρωθεν ἔχοντα
last_rejected.why: Source says 'having its underlying substance and its being/essence from elsewhere'—'being' is ambiguous; 'essence' or 'substance' clearer.
last_rejected.fix: having its underlying matter and its essence from elsewhere
last_rejected.ruling: 'being' for οὐσίαν is standard; 'substance' already precedes it. Ambiguity is minor, not misleading.
